question.text: How are option strategies for exporters different from importers in currency markets?

answer.text: Exporters with USD receivables sell USDINR futures or buy USDINR puts. Importers with USD payables buy USDINR futures or buy USDINR calls. The strategies are mirror images because the underlying USD exposures are opposite
Both exporters and importers use the same strategies because they face the same risk
Exporters can only use futures; importers can only use options
Exporters buy USDINR calls; importers buy USDINR puts

explanation.text: The Logic: NISM Series I pages 96-97 explain that an exporter receiving USD fears USDINR falling and hedges by selling USDINR futures or buying USDINR puts. An importer paying USD fears USDINR rising and hedges by buying USDINR futures or buying USDINR calls (pages 117 and 119). The exporter and importer therefore use mirror-image strategies for opposite underlying exposures. The Trap: Both parties do not face the same risk — they face opposite USD exposures and so use opposite hedges. Both can use futures or options. Buying USDINR calls as an exporter (or buying USDINR puts as an importer) would add to the existing exposure rather than reducing it. Note: The source uses long puts and long calls (and outright futures positions) as the standard exporter/importer hedges. Naked short calls or short puts are income strategies rather than hedges and are not the equivalents described on pages 96-97, 117 and 119.
